introduction-what-is-software-architectu.core: Software architecture is the set of significant, hard-to-change decisions: how a system is split into components, how they communicate, where data lives and which qualities (scalability, availability, maintainability, cost) are prioritised. Good architecture makes the important changes cheap and the system's trade-offs explicit.

first_principles.problem: A team picks microservices because 'everyone does', then drowns in deployment and debugging complexity.
truths: Every structure trades some qualities for others.
Early decisions constrain later ones.
Team structure shapes system structure (Conway's law).

analogy.title: A city plan
analogy.story: Where roads, districts and utilities go decides how easily the city grows.
analogy.breaks: Cities are hard to rebuild; software can be refactored, though at real cost.

code.text:
# ADR-007: Use a modular monolith
## Context: 8 engineers, unclear domain boundaries
## Decision: single deployable with enforced module boundaries
## Consequences: simple ops now; extract services when boundaries stabilise

check.a: Systems tend to mirror the communication structure of the organisations that build them.

the-monolith-all-eggs-in-one-basket.core: A monolith is one deployable unit containing all functionality, usually with one database. It's simple to develop, test, deploy and debug early on, with fast in-process calls and easy transactions. As it grows, coupling, slow builds, scaling everything together and coordinated deployments across many teams become painful.

first_principles.problem: A 200-engineer company deploys one giant app weekly, and any bug blocks every team's release.
truths: In-process calls are fast and reliable.
Shared code invites coupling.
One deployable means shared release cadence.
derivation: Start with a **monolith** for small teams and unclear domains.
Watch for **pain signals** (deploy contention, build time).

analogy.title: A single large department store
analogy.story: Everything under one roof is convenient, until renovating one floor closes the whole store.
analogy.breaks: Stores can close sections; monolith deploys usually affect everything.

check.q: Name one major benefit of a monolith for a small team.
check.a: Simplicity: fast in-process calls, easy local transactions, one thing to deploy and debug.

the-modular-monolith-the-organized-middl.core: A modular monolith is a single deployable divided into well-bounded modules with explicit interfaces, private internals and (ideally) separate schemas or tables per module. You keep monolith simplicity while gaining clean boundaries that make later extraction into services straightforward.

first_principles.problem: A monolith has become a 'big ball of mud' where any module calls any other's internals.
truths: Boundaries matter more than deployment units.
Enforced rules prevent coupling.
Extracting clean modules is much easier.

analogy.title: A house with well-defined rooms and doors
analogy.story: Everything is under one roof, but you don't walk through the bathroom to reach the kitchen.
analogy.breaks: Walls are physical; code boundaries need tooling to stop people tunnelling through.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Build fails if anyone reaches into billing internals.

check.q: Why is a modular monolith a good stepping stone to microservices?
check.a: Clean module boundaries and data ownership make extracting a module into a service straightforward.

microservices-divide-and-conquer.core: Microservices split a system into independently deployable services, each owning its data and a business capability, communicating over the network. They enable team autonomy, independent scaling and technology choice, but bring distributed-systems costs: network failures, eventual consistency, observability, versioning and operational overhead.

first_principles.problem: Teams step on each other in a shared codebase and can't release or scale independently.
truths: Independent deployability enables autonomy.
Network calls fail and add latency.
Shared databases recreate coupling.

analogy.title: A food court instead of one restaurant
analogy.story: Each stall runs independently with its own kitchen, but customers now walk between stalls.
analogy.breaks: Food courts share a seating area; services shouldn't share databases.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Teams deploy independently; must handle partial failures.

check.q: Why should microservices avoid sharing a database?
check.a: A shared database couples services' schemas and deployments, undermining independence.

a-note-on-soa-service-oriented-architect.core: Service-Oriented Architecture (2000s) also decomposed systems into services, but typically with coarse-grained enterprise services, heavyweight standards (SOAP, WS-*), and a central Enterprise Service Bus handling routing, transformation and orchestration. Microservices kept the service idea but favoured smart endpoints and dumb pipes, decentralised data and lightweight protocols.

first_principles.problem: Engineers dismiss microservices as 'SOA rebranded' or repeat SOA's ESB mistakes.
truths: Centralised integration logic becomes a bottleneck.
Heavy standards slow change.
Service boundaries are a lasting idea.
derivation: Keep **logic in services**, not the bus.

analogy.title: A central switchboard operator versus direct dialling
analogy.story: The operator knew everyone and became overloaded; direct dialling scales.
analogy.breaks: Operators added human flexibility; ESBs added complexity few could change.

example.title: Integration styles
flow: SOA: Order → ESB transforms & routes → Billing
Microservices: Order publishes OrderPlaced → Billing consumes

check.q: What does 'smart endpoints and dumb pipes' mean?
check.a: Business logic lives in services, while the communication layer just transports messages.

communication-event-driven-architecture-.core: In event-driven architecture, services publish events (facts that happened) to a broker, and interested services subscribe and react asynchronously. This decouples producers from consumers in time and knowledge, absorbs load spikes and makes adding new consumers easy, at the cost of eventual consistency, harder debugging and the need for idempotency and schema governance.

first_principles.problem: Order creation synchronously calls five services; if one is slow, checkout fails.
truths: Facts can be broadcast.
Async boundaries isolate failures.
Delivery may be duplicated or delayed.

analogy.title: A town crier
analogy.story: The crier announces news; whoever cares acts on it, without the crier knowing who listened.
analogy.breaks: Town criers speak once; brokers can retain and replay events.

example.title: Checkout decoupled
flow: Order service saves order, publishes OrderPlaced

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Checkout latency independent of downstream services.

check.q: What's a key trade-off of event-driven architecture?
check.a: Looser coupling and resilience in exchange for eventual consistency and harder debugging.

coordination-orchestration-vs-choreograp.core: Multi-step business processes can be orchestrated (a central coordinator such as a workflow engine like Temporal or Step Functions tells each service what to do and tracks state) or choreographed (services react to each other's events with no central controller). Orchestration is easier to understand and change; choreography is more decoupled but harder to see end to end.

first_principles.problem: An order process spread across event handlers is impossible to follow when something goes wrong.
truths: Processes need visibility.
Central control can be a bottleneck.
Events reduce coupling.

analogy.title: An orchestra conductor versus a dance troupe
analogy.story: The conductor directs every section; dancers react to each other's moves.
analogy.breaks: Dancers rehearse together; choreographed services are often built by teams who never meet.

example.title: Order saga orchestrated
flow: Workflow: reserve inventory → charge payment → create shipment

check.q: What's the main downside of choreography for complex processes?
check.a: No single place shows the end-to-end flow, making it hard to understand and debug.
